title: Review: Enthalpy change, exo/endothermic and profiles; Standard enthalpies of formation and combustion; Hess's law cycles; Bond enthalpies
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EN03#t2 term and clue written for the game; EN05#t1 term and clue written for the game; EN05#t2 term and clue written for the game; EN03#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN01#N.4a, EN03#N.10a, EN04#N.9a, EN05#N.6, EN01#N.11a, EN04#N.10, EN01#N.7a, EN01#N.13. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Endothermic
items.clue: Describes the breaking of a bond: energy is absorbed.

items.label: Standard state
items.clue: The pure, normal form of a substance under the reference conditions, e.g. Br₂(l).

items.label: Enthalpy of formation
items.clue: ΔH when exactly 1 mol of a compound is made from its elements; zero for an element.

items.label: Bond enthalpy
items.clue: Energy needed to break 1 mol of one type of link between atoms, all species gaseous.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the temperature of a substance?

options.text: The form of energy that flows from a hot object to a cold one
A measure of the total kinetic energy of all the particles it has
A quantity that has to rise whenever heat is transferred into it
A measure of the average kinetic energy of its particles

questions.explanation: Temperature is an average over the particles. It does not depend on how many there are, and it is not itself energy that is transferred.

questions.stem: CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g), ΔH = −99 kJ mol⁻¹. Bond enthalpies / kJ mol⁻¹: C–H 413, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432. What value for the C–Cl bond enthalpy do these data give?
questions.explanation: One C–H and one Cl–Cl break (656 kJ); one C–Cl and one H–Cl form. 656 − (x + 432) = −99, so x = 323 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Use the enthalpy changes of reactions 1 and 2 to calculate ΔH for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Reaction 1: H₂(g) + O₂(g) → H₂O₂(l), ΔH₁ = −187.8 kJ mol⁻¹. Reaction 2: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), ΔH₂ = −571.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.explanation: Reverse and double reaction 1: +375.6. Add reaction 2: −571.6. 2H₂ and one O₂ cancel. ΔH = −196.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol?
questions.explanation: 1 mol of ethanol burns completely to CO₂(g) and H₂O(l). Check: 7 O atoms on each side.

questions.stem: An enthalpy profile for a reaction shows, relative to the same zero, the reactants at 150 kJ mol⁻¹, the top of the energy barrier at 280 kJ mol⁻¹ and the products at 40 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for the reaction?
questions.explanation: ΔH = products − reactants = 40 − 150 = −110 kJ mol⁻¹. Products below reactants: exothermic.

questions.stem: Graphite turns into diamond only at enormous pressures, so ΔH for C(s, graphite) → C(s, diamond) can't be measured directly. But both forms burn. (1) C(s, graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ · (2) C(s, diamond) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −395.4 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for graphite → diamond?
questions.explanation: Keep (1); reverse (2), so its ΔH becomes +395.4. Add: CO₂ and O₂ cancel. ΔH = −393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: A mixture of iron and sulfur must be heated strongly before it reacts. Once started, it glows red-hot with no further heating. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is endothermic, because it needs heating to start.
The reaction is endothermic at first, then becomes exothermic once it starts.
The reaction is exothermic; the heating just gets it started.
Neither: the glow is the heat supplied at the start being given back.

questions.explanation: Most reactions need energy to get started, the activation energy. This one then releases more energy than it took in, so it keeps itself going: exothermic.

questions.stem: Hydrated barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride, both solids, are mixed in a flask standing on a wet wooden block. Within a minute the water under the flask freezes, sticking the flask to the block. Which statement about the reacting chemicals is correct?

options.text: They lose energy to the water, which then freezes; ΔH is negative.
They release "cold", which spreads into the water and freezes it; ΔH is positive.
Energy is used up as the solids react, so the water freezes; ΔH is negative.
They gain energy from the water, flask and air; ΔH is positive.

questions.explanation: The surroundings cool because energy flows into the system. The system gains energy: endothermic, ΔH positive.
